$$
A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{4}{9}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

steps.markdown:
Remember that the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$
is given by $$ A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)} \begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}. $$ If $\det(A)=0,$ then $A^{-1}$ doesn't exist since we can't divide by zero. In fact, we have the following statement: > $A^{-1}$ exists if and only if $\det(A) \neq 0.$ A matrix that has an inverse is called **invertible**. Otherwise, the matrix doesn't have an inverse and is called **non-invertible**. A square matrix that is non-invertible is called **singular**.

is a singular matrix, calculate the value of $x.$

The matrix $B$ is singular if and only if $\det (B)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\det (B) & =(-3)\cdot (2x+7)-5\cdot (-x+1) \\  & =-6x-21+5x-5 \\  & =-x-26.\end{aligned}

steps.markdown: If $V=\begin{bmatrix}7 & y \\ 5 & y\end{bmatrix}$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value of $y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\det (V) & =7\cdot y-5\cdot y \\  & =7y-5y \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $y$ is $y=0.$

steps.markdown:
The matrix

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & n \\ n & -18\end{bmatrix}
$$

is singular. Find all values of $n$.
steps.solution:
A square matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero. Here,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\det(A)\\
=\left(-8\right)\left(-18\right)\\
{}-\left(n\right)\left(n\right)\\
=-n^2+144
\end{gathered}
$$

Set this determinant equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-n^2+144&=0\\
n^2&=144\\
n&=\pm 12
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, $n=-12$ and $n=12$.

steps.markdown:
Given a matrix $A = 
	\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix},$
we have been using the following formula to compute the inverse:

$$
A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad-bc}
	\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}
$$

To check that this formula is correct for a general matrix $A$, we need to verify that

$$
AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I_2.
$$

First, we compute $A^{-1}A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}\cdot A & =\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}ad-bc & 0 \\ 0 & -bc+ad\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $A A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot {A}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}ad-bc & 0 \\ 0 & -bc+ad\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have verified that

$$
AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I_2,
$$

and we can be sure that the given formula is the correct formula for $A^{-1}.$
